records.greek: Ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν ἵνα μὴ σκανδαλισθῆτε.
records.gloss: These things I have spoken to you so that not you may be caused to stumble.

L.1: These things I have spoken to you so that you may not be caused to stumble.

R.1: I am telling you this so that you will not stumble and fall away.

decisions.choice: be caused to stumble: be tripped up so as to fall away from faith
alternatives: be offended, have one's feelings hurt
decisions.reason: The verb σκανδαλισθῆτε pictures a stumbling block that trips someone so that they fall. In John it means losing hold of faith in Jesus, as when many disciples turned back after the hard words of 6:61, 66, where the same verb is used. Here the danger is the hatred and persecution just described: if it took them by surprise, they might give up.

decisions.choice: these things I have spoken: the warnings of 15:18-27 about the world's hatred
alternatives: the whole of the farewell talk
decisions.reason: "These things" looks back to what Jesus has just said about the world hating and persecuting them (15:18-25), and forward to the plain warning of verse 2. The same opening recurs through the talk (14:25; 15:11; 16:4, 25, 33). The perfect tense presents the warning as given and standing.

decisions.choice: stumble and fall away
decisions.reason: "Stumble" keeps the picture of the verb, as at 6:61, and "fall away" says what the picture means here (meaning decision m1). "Be offended" now means having one's feelings hurt, which is far too weak.

records.heading: Warning of persecution

records.greek: ἀποσυναγώγους ποιήσουσιν ὑμᾶς· ἀλλ’ ἔρχεται ὥρα ἵνα πᾶς ὁ ἀποκτείνας ὑμᾶς δόξῃ λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: Out-of-synagogue [ones] they will make you; but comes an hour that everyone the [one] having killed you will think service to offer to the God.

L.2: They will put you out of the synagogue; but an hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think [that they are] offering service to God.

R.2: They will throw you out of the synagogue. In fact, the time will come when anyone who kills you will think that they are serving God by doing it.

decisions.choice: put out of the synagogue: shut out of the community's worship and common life
decisions.reason: The same word as in 9:22 and 12:42, found in the New Testament only in John. The synagogue was where Jews gathered for prayer and the reading of Scripture and the center of a town's shared life, so to be put out of it was to be cut off from one's own people. What the man born blind suffered (9:34) and the rulers feared (12:42), Jesus now foretells for his disciples.

decisions.choice: they: those who hate Jesus and his followers (15:18-25), here those with authority over the synagogue
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. It carries on the "they" of 15:20-25, the world that hates Jesus. Only those with authority over a synagogue could put people out of it, as the leaders had agreed to do in 9:22. The text does not say more about who they will be. The disciples themselves are Jews, and so is Jesus.

decisions.choice: offer service to God: perform an act of worship, a sacred duty offered to God
decisions.reason: The noun λατρείαν is used of the worship of God, above all the service of the temple and its sacrifices (Romans 9:4; Hebrews 9:1, 6), and the verb προσφέρειν is the word for offering a sacrifice. The killers will think that killing Jesus's followers is itself worship pleasing to God. Saul of Tarsus is an example: he persecuted the church out of zeal for God (Acts 26:9-11; Galatians 1:13-14; Philippians 3:6).

decisions.choice: but an hour is coming when: not merely that, but worse; a time set for this to happen
alternatives: the hour of Jesus's death and glory
decisions.reason: The "but" here heightens: not only exclusion, but death. "An hour is coming" is the phrase of 4:21 and 5:25, a time that will surely come. It is not Jesus's own hour (12:23; 13:1) but the time when his followers will suffer, which verse 4 calls "their hour". The word ἵνα, usually "so that", here means "when", as in 12:23 and 13:1.

decisions.choice: everyone who kills you ... [that {{gender:they are|he is}}] (L); anyone who kills you ... {{gender:they are|he is}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Everyone who kills" is general and in principle includes anyone; the pronoun that English needs after it carries the gender setting. Literal brackets the words the Greek leaves unstated.

decisions.choice: put out of (L); expel from (B); throw out of (R); hour (L, B); time (R); sacred service (B); serving God (R)
decisions.reason: Each level uses the wording it used at 9:22, so readers see the same word. Literal and Balanced keep "hour", as at 4:21 and 5:25; Readable says "time", because "hour" sounds like sixty minutes. "Sacred service" shows that the killers think of their deed as worship (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: καὶ ταῦτα ποιήσουσιν ὅτι οὐκ ἔγνωσαν τὸν πατέρα οὐδὲ ἐμέ.
records.gloss: And these things they will do because not they knew the Father nor me.

L.3: And these things they will do because they have not known the Father nor Me.

R.3: They will do these things because they do not know the Father or Me.

decisions.choice: the root of persecution: not knowing the Father, and so not knowing the Son
decisions.reason: Jesus said the same in 15:21 and told his opponents that they knew neither him nor his Father (7:28; 8:19, 54-55). Those who kill in God's name (verse 2) show that they do not know him; to know the Father is to know the one he sent (14:7; 17:3).

decisions.choice: have not known: they have never come to know them
alternatives: did not recognize them at a particular moment
decisions.reason: The past tense ἔγνωσαν looks at their whole relation to God and to Jesus: they never came to know them. This is a settled state, not one mistake.

decisions.choice: they will do (SBLGNT)
alternatives: they will do to you (many manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "to you" after "they will do", making plain who suffers, as 15:21 has it. Important early manuscripts lack it. The meaning is the same. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: have never known (B); do not know (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the settled state of the past tense with "never" (meaning decision m2). Readable uses the present, the plain way to say what is true of them now.

records.greek: ἀλλὰ ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν ἵνα ὅταν ἔλθῃ ἡ ὥρα αὐτῶν μνημονεύητε αὐτῶν ὅτι ἐγὼ εἶπον ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: But these things I have spoken to you so that when comes the hour of them you may remember them, that I said to you.

L.4: But these things I have spoken to you so that when their hour comes you may remember them, that I told [them] to you.

R.4: But I have warned you about these things, so that when they happen, you will remember that I told you.

decisions.choice: their hour: the time when these things happen
alternatives: the hour of the persecutors, their time of power (compare Luke 22:53, "this is your hour")
decisions.reason: "Their" is plural and most naturally points back to "these things" at the start of the sentence, the same word as "them" in "remember them". The hour is the time foretold in verse 2. It could refer to the persecutors, whose "hour" would be the time they are allowed to act, but "these things" are the nearer and more likely antecedent.

decisions.choice: remember them, that I told you: remember that Jesus told them beforehand
decisions.reason: The Greek says "remember them, that I told you": the object is named first, then what about it is to be remembered. The "I" is emphatic: it was Jesus himself who warned them. When persecution comes, it will not shake their faith but confirm what he said, as in 13:19 and 14:29.

decisions.choice: the hour of them (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts lack the first "their", reading "when the hour comes". The sense is little changed. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: when the hour for them comes (B); warned you ... when they happen (R)
decisions.reason: In English "their" would point to the persecutors of verse 3, so Balanced says "the hour for them", that is, for these things (meaning decision m1). Readable says it plainly, and "warned" is what "told you" means here. Literal brackets the object English needs after "told".

records.greek: Ταῦτα δὲ ὑμῖν ἐξ ἀρχῆς οὐκ εἶπον, ὅτι μεθ’ ὑμῶν ἤμην.
records.gloss: These things but to you from [the] beginning not I said, because with you I was.

L.4: And these things I did not say to you from [the] beginning, because I was with you.

R.4: I did not tell you these things at the beginning, because I was here with you.

decisions.choice: from the beginning: since Jesus first called them
alternatives: the beginning of creation, as in 1:1
decisions.reason: As in 15:27, the beginning is the start of Jesus's work with his disciples (1:35-51). The phrase is close but not identical: there ἐξ is a different preposition, with the same sense.

decisions.choice: while Jesus was with them, he drew the hostility on himself and kept them; now that he is leaving, they need to be told
alternatives: Jesus had never spoken of persecution before
decisions.reason: Jesus had kept and guarded them while he was with them (17:12), and at his arrest he will ask that they be let go (18:8-9); the world's hostility fell on him. Now he is going, and they will face it without him there in person, so he tells them what is coming. Other Gospels record earlier warnings of persecution (Matthew 10:17-22); "these things" here may mean the full warning given now, with the promise of the Advocate that goes with it.

decisions.choice: here with you
decisions.reason: Readable adds "here" to show that Jesus means his bodily presence among them, now ending.

records.heading: The work of the Advocate

records.greek: νῦν δὲ ὑπάγω πρὸς τὸν πέμψαντά με καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐρωτᾷ με· Ποῦ ὑπάγεις;
records.gloss: Now but I go to the [one] having sent me, and none of you asks me, "Where do you go?"

L.5: But now I am going to the one who sent Me, and none of you asks Me, 'Where are You going?'

R.5: But now I am going back to the Father, who sent Me. Yet not one of you is asking Me, 'Where are You going?'

decisions.choice: none of you asks: at this moment, none of them is asking where he goes; they think only of their own loss
alternatives: the farewell talks were joined from different occasions, and this was once spoken before 13:36 and 14:5
decisions.reason: Peter has asked "Lord, where are you going?" (13:36), and Thomas has said "we do not know where you are going" (14:5). The verb here is present: now, as Jesus speaks of going to the Father, none of them asks about it. Their earlier questions were about being left behind, and verse 6 says what fills them now: sorrow. If they asked where he is going, they would learn that he goes to the Father, which is reason for gladness (14:28). Another explanation is that the farewell talks were put together from more than one occasion. The text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: I am going to the one who sent me: Jesus's return to the Father, through his death
decisions.reason: "The one who sent me" is the Father (5:37; 7:33). Jesus came from the Father and goes back to him (13:3; 16:28). The present tense presents the going as already under way.

decisions.choice: going back to the Father, who sent me
alternatives: going to the one who sent me
decisions.reason: Readable names the Father, who in John is "the one who sent me" (meaning decision m2), and adds "back", since Jesus came from him. "Yet" shows the contrast the Greek "and" carries here.

records.greek: ἀλλ’ ὅτι ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν ἡ λύπη πεπλήρωκεν ὑμῶν τὴν καρδίαν.
records.gloss: But because these things I have spoken to you the sorrow has filled your the heart.

L.6: But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.

R.6: Instead, you are full of sorrow, because I have told you these things.

decisions.choice: sorrow: grief and distress, here at the thought of losing Jesus
decisions.reason: The noun λύπη is grief or pain of heart. It recurs in 16:20-22, where Jesus says their sorrow will be turned into joy, like a woman's pain in childbirth. Here it is the grief of friends about to be left.

decisions.choice: but: instead of asking, they grieve; your heart: each one's heart
decisions.reason: The "but" sets their sorrow against the question they do not ask (verse 5). "Your" is plural and "heart" singular, as in 14:1 and 14:27: each of them inwardly. The perfect tense "has filled" describes their state now.

decisions.choice: Instead (B, R); your hearts (B); you are full of sorrow (R)
decisions.reason: "Instead" shows what the "but" contrasts (meaning decision m2). Balanced makes "hearts" plural, the natural way to speak of many people's hearts, as at 14:27. Readable puts the result first in plain words.

records.greek: ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγω ὑμῖν, συμφέρει ὑμῖν ἵνα ἐγὼ ἀπέλθω.
records.gloss: But I the truth say to you, it is profitable for you that I go away.

L.7: But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away.

R.7: But this is the truth: it is better for you that I am going away.

decisions.choice: it is to your advantage: it is for your good, it works to your benefit
decisions.reason: The verb συμφέρει means to be useful or profitable. Jesus's going away seems the worst thing that could happen to them; he says it is for their good, and verse 7b gives the reason.

decisions.choice: the same words as Caiaphas: "it is to your advantage that"
decisions.reason: Caiaphas said to the council that it was to their advantage that one man should die for the people (11:50; recalled in 18:14), using the same verb with "to you" and "that". John has said that Caiaphas spoke more truly than he knew (11:51-52). Here Jesus himself says that his departure, which comes through that death, is to his disciples' advantage.

decisions.choice: I tell you the truth: an emphatic assurance against what they feel
decisions.reason: The "I" is emphatic, and the truth is put first: whatever their sorrow tells them, this is the truth. Truth is a key term.

decisions.choice: it is to your advantage (L); my going away is to your advantage (B); it is better for you (R)
decisions.reason: Each level uses the wording it used for Caiaphas's words at 11:50, so readers can hear the echo (meaning decision m2). Balanced makes "my going away" the subject, which keeps the stress on the going.

records.greek: ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ ἀπέλθω, ὁ παράκλητος οὐ μὴ ἔλθῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς· ἐὰν δὲ πορευθῶ, πέμψω αὐτὸν πρὸς ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: If for not I go away, the advocate not not will come to you; if but I go, I will send him to you.

L.7: For if I do not go away, the Advocate will certainly not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you.

R.7: If I do not leave, the Advocate will never come to you. But if I do go, I will send Him to you.

decisions.choice: the Advocate: one called to stand beside another and speak for them
decisions.reason: The word παράκλητος was used of someone called to stand by a person, above all in a court. It is the same title as in 14:16, 14:26 and 15:26, the Holy Spirit. The next verses show him in a court setting: he will prove the world wrong (verses 8-11).

decisions.choice: the Spirit is given when Jesus has gone to the Father
decisions.reason: John has already said that the Spirit had not yet been given because Jesus had not yet been glorified (7:39). Jesus must go by way of the cross to the Father before he sends the Advocate. The risen Jesus breathes on his disciples and says "Receive the Holy Spirit" (20:22).

decisions.choice: will certainly not come: a strong double negative; I will send him: Jesus himself sends the Advocate
decisions.reason: The two negatives οὐ μὴ together make the strongest denial Greek has. In 14:16, 26 the Father gives and sends the Advocate; here and in 15:26 Jesus sends him. The two verbs for going, ἀπέλθω and πορευθῶ, mean the same here. The masculine pronoun αὐτὸν agrees with the masculine word for Advocate.

decisions.choice: the Advocate
decisions.reason: The book uses "the Advocate" at every level, because John's setting is testimony and judgment (meaning decision m1). Other well-known renderings are Helper, Counselor and Comforter; each catches part of the sense.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The Spirit is never "it" in this translation. "Him" takes the deity pronoun setting like every pronoun for God. Literal shows the double negative with "certainly", Balanced with "at all" and Readable with "never" (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: καὶ ἐλθὼν ἐκεῖνος ἐλέγξει τὸν κόσμον περὶ ἁμαρτίας καὶ περὶ δικαιοσύνης καὶ περὶ κρίσεως·
records.gloss: And having come that one will convict the world concerning sin and concerning righteousness and concerning judgment;

L.8: And when He has come, He will convict the world concerning sin and concerning righteousness and concerning judgment:

R.8: When He comes, He will show the world that it is wrong about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment.

decisions.choice: convict: expose and prove wrong, as a case is proved in court
alternatives: convince, bring to inner conviction and repentance
decisions.reason: The verb ἐλέγξει means to bring something into the open and prove it, to show someone in the wrong. In 3:20 evil deeds are exposed by the light; in 8:46 Jesus asks who can prove him guilty of sin. The setting here is a trial: the world has judged Jesus, and the Advocate reopens the case and shows the world to be wrong. The word does not say whether the world will accept the verdict. Some will be convinced and believe; others will stand condemned. The Spirit does this through the disciples' testimony (15:26-27).

decisions.choice: the world: humanity organized against God
decisions.reason: As in 15:18-19, the world is people as they set themselves against God and his messenger. It has hated Jesus (15:18) and will hate his disciples.

decisions.choice: three heads of the charge, each explained in the verses that follow
decisions.reason: Sin, righteousness and judgment are three points on which the world is shown to be in the wrong; verses 9, 10 and 11 each give a reason with "because". Righteousness is a key term. The masculine ἐκεῖνος ("that one", "he") agrees with the Advocate of verse 7.

decisions.choice: show the world to be in the wrong (B); show the world that it is wrong (R)
decisions.reason: "Convict" in English now suggests a verdict of guilty in court, which fits sin but not righteousness. Balanced and Readable say what the verb does in all three cases: it proves the world wrong (meaning decision m1). The footnote gives "convict".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: The Advocate is never "it". "He" takes the deity pronoun setting. Literal says "he" for the emphatic "that one", as at 14:26 and 15:26.

records.greek: περὶ ἁμαρτίας μέν, ὅτι οὐ πιστεύουσιν εἰς ἐμέ·
records.gloss: concerning sin on the one hand, because not they believe in me;

L.9: concerning sin, because they do not believe in Me;

R.9: It is wrong about sin, because people do not believe in Me.

decisions.choice: about sin: the world is wrong about what sin is and guilty of it, for its sin is not believing in Jesus
alternatives: the Spirit convicts people of their sins in general, and unbelief is the evidence
the world sins in that it does not believe
decisions.reason: In John the sin above all others is refusing to believe in the one God sent: "unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins" (8:24; compare 3:18-19; 9:41; 15:22, 24). The world thought Jesus was the sinner (9:24). The Spirit shows that the guilt lies with those who will not believe in him. The word ὅτι can mean "because" or "in that"; either way unbelief is the heart of the world's sin.

decisions.choice: they: the people of the world
decisions.reason: The plural verb takes "the world" of verse 8 as the people in it.

decisions.choice: about sin ... ; about righteousness ... ; about judgment ... (verses 9-11 continue one sentence)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps verses 8 to 11 as one English sentence, with each verse taking up one of the three points, as the Greek does.

decisions.choice: It is wrong about sin; people
decisions.reason: Readable makes each of verses 9 to 11 a sentence, repeating "it is wrong about" from verse 8, and says "people" for the plural "they" (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: περὶ δικαιοσύνης δέ, ὅτι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ὑπάγω καὶ οὐκέτι θεωρεῖτέ με·
records.gloss: concerning righteousness and, because to the Father I go and no longer you see me;

L.10: and concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you no longer see Me;

R.10: It is wrong about righteousness, because I am going away to the Father, and you will not see Me anymore.

decisions.choice: about righteousness: the world was wrong about who is righteous; Jesus's going to the Father shows that God has vindicated him
alternatives: the world's own righteousness is shown to be false
the righteousness God gives is made available through Jesus's going
decisions.reason: The world judged Jesus a sinner and put him to death as one (9:24; 18:30; 19:7). His going to the Father, through death and resurrection, is God's verdict that he was in the right; he goes to the one who sent him, which no sinner could do. The world's own claim to righteousness is shown up by the same verdict. John uses the word δικαιοσύνης only here and in verse 8, so its sense must be taken from this context. Righteousness is a key term.

decisions.choice: you no longer see me: the disciples, addressed directly; Jesus will no longer be with them as before
decisions.reason: The verse moves from "they" (the world) to "you" (the disciples). Jesus's going means that even they will not see him as they do now; the righteousness that is his is now hidden with the Father, and the Advocate makes it known. Yet in verse 16 he adds that in a little while they will see him again. The present θεωρεῖτέ is used of what is about to be true.

decisions.choice: you will see me no longer (B); you will not see me anymore (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the future for the present tense that looks to what is about to happen (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: περὶ δὲ κρίσεως, ὅτι ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου τούτου κέκριται.
records.gloss: concerning but judgment, because the ruler of the world this has been judged.

L.11: and concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.

R.11: And it is wrong about judgment, because Satan, the ruler of this world, has already been judged.

decisions.choice: about judgment: the world judged Jesus, but in truth its ruler is the one judged
alternatives: the world will face God's judgment at the end
the Spirit shows what true judgment is
decisions.reason: The world condemned Jesus, and so passed judgment wrongly (7:24; 8:15). At the cross the verdict is turned around: "now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out" (12:31). The ruler who seemed to win at the cross has been condemned there. So the world's judgment is shown to be false, and the world under that ruler stands judged with him.

decisions.choice: the ruler of this world: Satan
decisions.reason: The same title as in 12:31 and 14:30. He is the devil, who put the betrayal into Judas's heart (13:2, 27).

decisions.choice: has been judged: a perfect tense; the verdict is already given, though the cross is still ahead
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks from the point of view of the Advocate's coming, when the cross is past, and of his own certainty that the hour has come (12:31, "now"). The perfect κέκριται means the verdict is given and stands.

decisions.choice: and about judgment
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "and" before the last of the three points, as English lists do; Literal has it too, where the Greek has a joining "but". Balanced says "stands judged" for the perfect tense: the verdict is given and remains (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: Satan, the ruler of this world; already
decisions.reason: As at 12:31 and 14:30, Readable names Satan, whom the title means (meaning decision m2); Jesus is the speaker, and he knows who the ruler is. Every level keeps "the ruler of this world" as at 12:31. "Already" brings out the perfect tense (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: Ἔτι πολλὰ ἔχω ὑμῖν λέγειν, ἀλλ’ οὐ δύνασθε βαστάζειν ἄρτι·
records.gloss: Still many things I have to you to say, but not you are able to bear now;

L.12: I have many things still to say to you, but you are not able to bear [them] now.

R.12: I have much more to tell you, but right now it would be too much for you.

decisions.choice: bear: carry a load; here, take in and endure what he would say
decisions.reason: The verb βαστάζειν means to carry something heavy (19:17, of Jesus carrying his cross). What Jesus still has to say would be too heavy for them now, in their sorrow and before his death and resurrection. Only after he was raised did they understand what he had said and done (2:22; 12:16).

decisions.choice: many things still to say: what the Spirit will make known (verses 13-15)
alternatives: new teaching beyond what Jesus taught
decisions.reason: Verses 13-15 say how these things will be told: the Spirit will take what is Jesus's and declare it. So the "many things" are not a different message, but a fuller understanding of Jesus and what is to come (14:26).

decisions.choice: more than you can bear right now (B); it would be too much for you (R)
alternatives: you are not able to bear [them] now (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the weight the subject, which is how English says this. "Right now" carries the stress the Greek puts on "now": it will not always be so.

records.greek: ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ἐκεῖνος, τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας, ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πάσῃ, οὐ γὰρ λαλήσει ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ, ἀλλ’ ὅσα ἀκούσει λαλήσει, καὶ τὰ ἐρχόμενα ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: When but comes that one, the Spirit of the truth, he will guide you in the truth all; not for he will speak from himself, but as much as he will hear he will speak, and the things coming he will declare to you.

L.13: But when He comes, the Spirit of truth, He will guide you in all the truth; for He will not speak from Himself, but whatever He hears He will speak, and the things that are coming He will declare to you.

R.13: But the Spirit of truth will come, and when He does, He will guide you in all the truth. His words will not come from Himself. He will say only what He hears, and He will tell you about the things that are still to come.

decisions.choice: "that one", masculine, then "the Spirit", neuter, in apposition: the Advocate spoken of as a person
alternatives: the neuter means the Spirit is an impersonal force
the masculine is a deliberate statement that the Spirit is a person
decisions.reason: The pronoun ἐκεῖνος is masculine, carrying on the Advocate of verses 7-8, and then "the Spirit of truth" is added, a neuter noun, to say who he is. Grammar explains the masculine, so it does not prove a point on its own, and the neuter noun says nothing about whether the Spirit is a thing (as in 14:17, 26). What shows him as a person is what he does here: he guides, hears, speaks, declares and glorifies.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of truth: the Holy Spirit, who comes from the God of truth and makes the truth known
alternatives: a spirit or attitude of truthfulness
decisions.reason: This is the Advocate already named "the Spirit of truth" (14:17; 15:26) and "the Holy Spirit" (14:26). He leads into the truth that Jesus is (14:6). Truth is a key term.

decisions.choice: in all the truth (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "into all the truth", with a different preposition and word order; important early manuscripts have "in all the truth", as the SBLGNT does. The difference is slight: "in" pictures guidance within the whole of the truth, "into" a leading toward it. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: he will not speak from himself: the Spirit's message comes from the Father and the Son
decisions.reason: Jesus says the same of himself: he does not speak on his own, but what the Father has taught him (7:16-18; 8:28; 12:49; 14:10). The Spirit likewise speaks what he hears; verses 14-15 say that what he hears and takes is Jesus's, and all that is Jesus's is the Father's. The SBLGNT has the future "will hear"; some manuscripts have the present "hears", with the same sense.

decisions.choice: the things that are coming: what was still ahead for the disciples, beginning with Jesus's death and resurrection and the life of the church that followed
alternatives: only events at the end of the age
decisions.reason: The phrase is open. From where the disciples stand the coming things begin with the hour now at hand; the Spirit will show them what these mean, and what is to follow. The verb ἀναγγελεῖ ("declare, announce") was used by the Samaritan woman of the Messiah: "he will declare all things to us" (4:25). Here it is the Spirit who declares.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} for the Spirit
decisions.reason: The Spirit is never "it" in this translation. The Greek pronoun and verbs agree with the Advocate, a masculine noun, and the Spirit is a person (meaning decision m1), so every level says "he" and "himself", with the deity pronoun setting as for the Father and the Son. A sentence that starts with "He" or "His" has the capital either way and needs no setting.

decisions.choice: when he, the Spirit of truth, comes (B); the Spirit of truth will come, and when he does (R); what he says will not come from himself (B); his words will not come from himself (R)
alternatives: when he comes, the Spirit of truth (Literal)
he will not speak from himself (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the name next to the pronoun it explains; Readable uses the name alone. "From himself" means "on his own": Balanced and Readable say that his words do not start with him (meaning decision m4). Readable adds "only", which the contrast with "not from himself" implies.

records.greek: ἐκεῖνος ἐμὲ δοξάσει, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἐμοῦ λήμψεται καὶ ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: That one me will glorify, because from the mine he will take and will declare to you.

L.14: He will glorify Me, because He will take from what is Mine and will declare [it] to you.

R.14: He will bring glory to Me. He will take what belongs to Me and tell it to you.

decisions.choice: he will glorify me: the Spirit makes Jesus known for who he is
decisions.reason: To glorify is to show someone's true worth and greatness. The Spirit does not draw attention to himself; he makes known Jesus, who is glorified in his death, resurrection and return to the Father (12:23; 13:31-32; 17:1, 5). The "me" stands first for emphasis. Glorify is a key term.

decisions.choice: take from what is mine: draw on what belongs to Jesus, his words, his work and all that he is
decisions.reason: The Greek has "from the mine", meaning from what is Jesus's own. Verse 15 explains how much that is: all that the Father has.

decisions.choice: He (plain at sentence start); {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will take; {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}
decisions.reason: The Spirit is "he", never "it". The sentence opens with plain "He", which is capitalised either way; the later "he" carries the deity pronoun setting like every pronoun for God. "Me" and "mine" are Jesus speaking of himself and take the setting too.

decisions.choice: receive ... make it known (B); bring glory to; take what belongs to me and tell it (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "receive", since the Spirit takes what is given him, and "make known" for the verb "declare". Readable says "bring glory to", keeping the key word glory, and uses everyday words for the rest.

records.greek: πάντα ὅσα ἔχει ὁ πατὴρ ἐμά ἐστιν· διὰ τοῦτο εἶπον ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἐμοῦ λαμβάνει καὶ ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: All things as many as has the Father mine are; because of this I said that from the mine he takes and will declare to you.

L.15: All things whatever the Father has are Mine; because of this I said that He takes from what is Mine and will declare [it] to you.

R.15: Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to Me. That is why I said the Spirit will take what belongs to Me and tell it to you.

decisions.choice: all that the Father has is mine: the Son shares everything with the Father
decisions.reason: The Father has given all things into the Son's hands (3:35; 13:3), and in his prayer Jesus says, "all mine are yours, and yours are mine" (17:10). So when the Spirit takes from what is Jesus's, he makes known what is the Father's too: the Father, the Son and the Spirit work as one.

decisions.choice: he takes: a present tense where verse 14 has the future "he will take"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads the present λαμβάνει here; some manuscripts have the future, as in verse 14. The present may describe what the Spirit does as a settled pattern, or a future that is certain. The meaning is the same as verse 14. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: will receive (B); will take (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat the future of verse 14, which this verse quotes (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps the present.

decisions.choice: the Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable names the Spirit for "he", since the nearest person named is the Father.

records.greek: Μικρὸν καὶ οὐκέτι θεωρεῖτέ με, καὶ πάλιν μικρὸν καὶ ὄψεσθέ με.
records.gloss: A little and no longer you see me, and again a little and you will see me.

L.16: A little [while] and you no longer see Me, and again a little [while] and you will see Me."

R.16: In a little while you will not see Me anymore. Then a little while after that, you will see Me again."

decisions.choice: two verbs for seeing, most likely for variety and because of the change of tense; both mean that the disciples will see Jesus
alternatives: the first verb means ordinary sight and the second a deeper seeing by faith
decisions.reason: The first "see" is θεωρεῖτέ (from θεωρέω), the second ὄψεσθέ, a future of ὁράω. The future of seeing was usually expressed with this second verb, so the change may simply follow the change of tense. John also uses the first verb for the disciples' seeing of Jesus after his death (14:19, "you see me"), so it does not stand only for bodily sight; and the second is used when the disciples see the risen Jesus (20:18, 20, 25, 29). Some readers find a contrast between seeing with the eyes and seeing with understanding, but John's usage does not clearly support it.

decisions.choice: the verse ends with "you will see me" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: adds "because I am going to the Father" (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, end the verse with "you will see me". Many later manuscripts add "because I am going to the Father", most likely taken from the disciples' question in verse 17, which joins this saying to the words of 16:10. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the two little whiles: first the short time until Jesus's death, then the short time until the disciples see him risen
alternatives: the second little while ends with the coming of the Spirit (14:16-19; 16:7)
the second little while ends with Jesus's return at the end of the age (14:3)
decisions.reason: Jesus is speaking on the night before his death, so the first little while is a matter of hours. The second ends when they see him again, and verses 20-22 describe that seeing as sorrow turned to joy; John tells it in those terms when the risen Jesus comes to them: "the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord" (20:20). In 14:18-19 the same words about seeing him are tied to his coming to them and to the gift of the Spirit, and the promised joy and asking in his name (16:22-24) reach beyond Easter into the life of the church, so some take the second little while of the Spirit's coming or of his final return. The Easter reading fits the closest words best, but the others cannot be ruled out.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself, "he" and "his" when the disciples or the narrator speak of him, and "he" for the Father. At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: In a little while ... after another little while (B); In a little while ... a little while after that ... again (R); "will no longer see" in the future
alternatives: In a short time (as Balanced has in 14:19)
decisions.reason: In 14:19 Balanced and Readable say "in a short time" and "soon". Here they keep "a little while", because the disciples puzzle over that very phrase in verses 17-19 ("What is this 'little while'?"), and the same words must recur. The present "you no longer see" speaks of what is about to happen, so Balanced and Readable put it in the future, as in 14:19. Readable adds "again" to the second clause, which "again a little while" implies.

records.heading: Sorrow will turn to joy

records.greek: εἶπαν οὖν ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ πρὸς ἀλλήλους· Τί ἐστιν τοῦτο ὃ λέγει ἡμῖν· Μικρὸν καὶ οὐ θεωρεῖτέ με, καὶ πάλιν μικρὸν καὶ ὄψεσθέ με;
records.gloss: Said therefore [some] of the disciples of him to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little and not you see me, and again a little and you will see me';

L.17: So [some] of His disciples said to one another, "What is this that He says to us, 'A little [while] and you do not see Me, and again a little [while] and you will see Me'?

R.17: Some of His disciples began asking each other, "What does He mean by saying, 'In a little while you will not see Me anymore. Then a little while after that, you will see Me again'?

decisions.choice: some of his disciples, not all of them
decisions.reason: The phrase "out of his disciples" (ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν) has no word for "some"; the preposition itself marks a part of the group, as in 7:40. They speak "to one another", not to Jesus: they want to ask him but hold back (verse 19; compare 16:5).

decisions.choice: the disciples repeat Jesus's saying of verse 16 word for word, with one small change that does not alter its sense
decisions.reason: In verse 16 Jesus said "no longer" (οὐκέτι); the disciples, and Jesus himself in verse 19, say simply "not" (οὐ). The rest is the same. The saying is repeated three times in four verses (16, 17, 19), which shows how much it puzzled them and fixes it in the reader's mind.

decisions.choice: the disciples cannot yet understand that Jesus speaks of his death and resurrection
decisions.reason: John often notes that the disciples understood Jesus's words only after he rose (2:22; 12:16; 20:9). Here their question shows the same thing from the inside: they hear the words but cannot see what event they point to.

decisions.choice: the quotation repeats the wording of verse 16 at Balanced and Readable; Literal has "you do not see" for the one changed word
decisions.reason: The disciples quote what Jesus has just said, so Balanced and Readable repeat verse 16 exactly, as the reader will recognise it. Literal shows the one word that changes (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable turn "What is this that he says" into "What does he mean", the natural English for asking about the sense of words.

records.greek: καί· Ὅτι ὑπάγω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα;
records.gloss: and, "Because I go to the Father"?"

L.17: And, 'Because I am going to the Father'?"

R.17: And what does He mean, 'because I am going to the Father'?"

decisions.choice: Ὅτι here means "because": the disciples quote Jesus's words of 16:10
alternatives: the word only introduces the quotation ("and, 'I am going to the Father'")
decisions.reason: This word often simply opens a quotation, and that is possible here. But 16:10 has the same words, "because I am going to the Father", and the disciples are putting together things Jesus has said in this discourse; they quote that phrase as he said it, reason word and all.

decisions.choice: going to the Father: Jesus's return to the Father through his death, resurrection and exaltation
decisions.reason: Jesus has spoken of his going to the Father again and again (13:1; 14:12, 28; 16:5, 10, 28). The disciples put this saying beside the one about the little while and cannot see how the two fit: how can he go away to the Father and also be seen again?

decisions.choice: And what about ... (B); And what does he mean, ... (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "and" before the second quoted saying; the question "What is this?" carries over from the first part. Balanced and Readable supply "what about" and "what does he mean" so that the second saying is plainly a second question.

records.greek: ἔλεγον οὖν· Τί ἐστιν τοῦτο ὃ λέγει μικρόν;
records.gloss: They were saying therefore, "What is this that he says, 'little'?

L.18: So they were saying, "What is this that He says, 'a little [while]'?

R.18: They kept asking, "What does He mean by 'a little while'?

decisions.choice: they were saying: they talked it over again and again
decisions.reason: The verb ἔλεγον is imperfect, the tense of continued or repeated action: the question went round among them.

decisions.choice: "little while" is what puzzles them most
decisions.reason: Of everything Jesus has said, they single out the phrase "a little while". They cannot tell what span of time he means, or what will happen at its end.

decisions.choice: kept saying (B); kept asking (R)
decisions.reason: "Kept saying" gives the sense of the continuing tense (meaning decision m1) in plain English. Readable says "asking", since what they say is a question.

records.greek: οὐκ οἴδαμεν τί λαλεῖ.
records.gloss: Not we know what he speaks."

L.18: We do not know what He is speaking [of]."

R.18: We do not understand what He is talking about."

decisions.choice: we do not know what he is speaking of: they cannot grasp his meaning
decisions.reason: They have heard the words; what they lack is their meaning. "Know" (οἴδαμεν) here is understanding, as when Jesus says that his disciples did not understand his words until later (13:7). Jesus will soon speak to them plainly (16:25, 29).

decisions.choice: do not understand
decisions.reason: In English "we do not know what he is talking about" can sound dismissive; "understand" says that they are puzzled, which is the sense (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἔγνω Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤθελον αὐτὸν ἐρωτᾶν, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Περὶ τούτου ζητεῖτε μετ’ ἀλλήλων ὅτι εἶπον· Μικρὸν καὶ οὐ θεωρεῖτέ με, καὶ πάλιν μικρὸν καὶ ὄψεσθέ με;
records.gloss: Knew Jesus that they were wanting him to ask, and he said to them, "About this are you seeking with one another, that I said, 'A little and not you see me, and again a little and you will see me'?"

L.19: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask Him, and He said to them, "Are you inquiring with one another about this, that I said, 'A little [while] and you do not see Me, and again a little [while] and you will see Me'?

R.19: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask Him about this. So He said to them, "Are you asking each other what I meant by these words: 'In a little while you will not see Me anymore. Then a little while after that, you will see Me again'?

decisions.choice: Jesus knew: he was aware of their wish before they spoke; John does not say how
alternatives: he noticed it from their talk among themselves
decisions.reason: Jesus may simply have seen them talking together. But John often says that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25; 6:61, 64; 13:11), and a few verses later the disciples say, "Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you" (16:30), which answers this very moment. John most likely means more than ordinary noticing, though the words alone do not say so.

decisions.choice: ask him: put a question to him; seeking with one another: discussing among themselves
decisions.reason: The verb for "ask" (ἐρωτᾶν, from ἐρωτάω) is the one for asking a question, and it returns in verse 23: "in that day you will ask me nothing". The verb ζητεῖτε means seeking, here seeking an answer together, talking it over.

decisions.choice: Jesus repeats his saying in the same words as the disciples did
decisions.reason: Jesus quotes himself with "not" instead of "no longer", exactly as the disciples did in verse 17. He does not explain the riddle directly; he answers with what the little whiles will bring: sorrow and then joy (verses 20-22).

decisions.choice: discussing with one another what I meant when I said (B); asking each other what I meant by these words (R); the quoted saying as in verse 16
alternatives: inquiring with one another about this, that I said (Literal)
decisions.reason: "About this ... that I said" is a Greek way of pointing to the words in question; Balanced says "what I meant when I said", Readable "what I meant by these words". The quoted saying is worded as in verse 16 so that readers recognise it.

records.greek: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι κλαύσετε καὶ θρηνήσετε ὑμεῖς, ὁ δὲ κόσμος χαρήσεται· ὑμεῖς λυπηθήσεσθε, ἀλλ’ ἡ λύπη ὑμῶν εἰς χαρὰν γενήσεται.
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you that will weep and will lament you, the but world will rejoice; you will be grieved, but the grief of you into joy will become.

L.20: Truly, truly I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be made sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.

R.20: I tell you the truth: you will cry and mourn, but the world will be glad. You will be very sad, but your sadness will turn into joy.

decisions.choice: weep and lament: loud mourning, the kind made for the dead
decisions.reason: "Weep" (κλαύσετε) is crying aloud, as Mary and the mourners wept for Lazarus (11:31, 33). "Lament" (θρηνήσετε) is the wailing of a funeral; Luke uses it of the women who mourned for Jesus on the way to the cross (Luke 23:27). Jesus is telling them that they will mourn him as one who has died.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity set against Jesus, which will be glad at his death
decisions.reason: As in 15:18-19, the world is set against the disciples: those who hate Jesus and want him gone. The stressed "you" and "the world" are put side by side: the same event will bring grief to one and gladness to the other.

decisions.choice: your sorrow will become joy: the same events that cause their grief will become the cause of their joy
alternatives: their sorrow will be replaced by joy
decisions.reason: The Greek says that the sorrow itself "will become" joy, not that joy will come after it. The death they mourn, once he is risen, becomes the ground of their joy. Verse 21 gives a picture of exactly this: the pain of childbirth issues in the joy of a new life.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it applies also in verse 23.

decisions.choice: weep and lament (L); weep and mourn aloud (B); cry and mourn (R); sorrow (L, B) and sadness (R) for the noun throughout verses 20-22
decisions.reason: Balanced says "mourn aloud" for the loud lament of mourners (meaning decision m1). The noun for sorrow occurs in verses 20, 21 and 22, and the link between them is the point of the picture, so Literal and Balanced say "sorrow" each time and Readable says "sad" or "sadness" in verses 20 and 22.

records.greek: ἡ γυνὴ ὅταν τίκτῃ λύπην ἔχει, ὅτι ἦλθεν ἡ ὥρα αὐτῆς· ὅταν δὲ γεννήσῃ τὸ παιδίον, οὐκέτι μνημονεύει τῆς θλίψεως διὰ τὴν χαρὰν ὅτι ἐγεννήθη ἄνθρωπος εἰς τὸν κόσμον.
records.gloss: The woman when she gives birth sorrow has, because came the hour of her; when but she has borne the child, no longer she remembers the affliction because of the joy that was born a human being into the world.

L.21: The woman, when she is giving birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.

R.21: When a woman is having a baby, she is in pain, because her time has come. But after the baby is born, she forgets all that pain. She is full of joy that a new person has come into the world.

decisions.choice: sorrow: the pain and distress of labor, called by the same word as the disciples' sorrow
decisions.reason: The noun λύπην usually means grief, but it is also used of bodily pain, and here it covers both. Jesus uses the same word for the disciples in verses 20 and 22, so that the woman's labor is a picture of their grief.

decisions.choice: her hour: the time for her child to be born
alternatives: a deliberate echo of Jesus's own hour
decisions.reason: In the picture, "her hour" is simply the time of giving birth. Yet "the hour" is John's word for the time of Jesus's death and glory (12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1), and the woman's hour stands for the disciples' hour of grief at that death. The plain sense is certain; how far John means the echo is not.

decisions.choice: ἄνθρωπος: a human being, a new person
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for a human being, not the word for a male. The point is not the child's sex but that a new human life has come into the world, which outweighs the pain.

decisions.choice: the pains of childbirth: a picture the prophets used for the distress that comes before God's new age
alternatives: an everyday picture with no particular passage in view
decisions.reason: The prophets compare Israel's suffering before God saves it to a woman in labor (Isaiah 26:17-19, where the picture ends in the dead rising; 66:7-14; Micah 4:9-10). Isaiah 66 also gives the words Jesus uses in verse 22 (66:14, "you will see, and your heart will rejoice"). The picture works on its own as everyday life; that John wants readers to hear the prophets as well is likely but not certain.

decisions.choice: sorrow (L, B), pain (R); anguish (L, B), all that pain (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "sorrow" for the same noun as in verses 20 and 22, so the link stays visible (meaning decision m1). Readable says "pain", which a young reader expects of childbirth. For the second noun, a word for pressure and distress, Literal and Balanced say "anguish".

decisions.choice: a woman (B, R); her hour (L, B), her time (R); a human being (L, B), a new person (R)
decisions.reason: The article with "woman" marks the general case, so Balanced and Readable say "a woman". Literal and Balanced keep "her hour" so that the echo of Jesus's hour can be heard (meaning decision m2); Readable says "her time". "A human being" is already inclusive, so no setting is needed; "a man" would suggest a male child, which the word does not mean (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν νῦν μὲν λύπην ἔχετε· πάλιν δὲ ὄψομαι ὑμᾶς, καὶ χαρήσεται ὑμῶν ἡ καρδία, καὶ τὴν χαρὰν ὑμῶν οὐδεὶς αἴρει ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: And you therefore now indeed sorrow have; again but I will see you, and will rejoice of you the heart, and the joy of you no one takes from you.

L.22: So you also now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and your joy no one takes from you.

R.22: It is the same for you. You are sad now. But I will see you again. Then your hearts will be full of gladness. No one will ever take your joy away from you.

decisions.choice: I will see you again: Jesus will come to them risen, and their grief will turn to gladness
decisions.reason: In verse 16 the disciples are the ones who will see; here Jesus is: he will come and see them. This happens on the evening of the resurrection, when he stands among them and "the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord" (20:19-20).

decisions.choice: your heart will rejoice: the words of Isaiah 66:14
decisions.reason: Isaiah 66 pictures Zion giving birth suddenly to a new people (66:7-9) and then says, "you will see, and your heart will rejoice" (66:14); the Greek translation of Isaiah has the same words as here. The labor picture of verse 21 and this promise come together from the same chapter. A reviewer should check the wording against the Greek of Isaiah.

decisions.choice: no one takes, present (αἴρει, SBLGNT)
alternatives: no one will take, future (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts have the future, "no one will take". The SBLGNT reads the present. The sense is nearly the same: the present states it as a settled fact. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: no one takes your joy: a joy beyond anyone's reach, from then on
decisions.reason: The present states what will always be so: unlike their sorrow, which lasts only a little while, the joy of seeing him again cannot be taken from them by the world or anyone else. "Your heart" is singular, the heart of each and of all together.

decisions.choice: your hearts (B, R); no one takes ... away (B); No one will ever take ... away (R); full of gladness (R)
decisions.reason: English says "hearts" for the heart of each of several people. Balanced keeps the present "takes", which in English can state a lasting fact; Readable says "will ever take" to make the lasting fact plain (meaning decision m4). Readable says "full of gladness" for the verb "rejoice", keeping "joy" for the noun.

records.greek: καὶ ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐμὲ οὐκ ἐρωτήσετε οὐδέν· ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἄν τι αἰτήσητε τὸν πατέρα δώσει ὑμῖν ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου.
records.gloss: And in that the day me not you will ask nothing; truly truly I say to you, if anything you ask the Father he will give to you in the name of me.

L.23: And in that day you will ask Me nothing. Truly, truly I say to you, if you ask the Father anything, He will give [it] to you in My name.

R.23: When that day comes, you will have no more questions to ask Me. I tell you the truth: if you ask the Father for anything, He will give it to you in My name.

decisions.choice: two verbs for asking: "ask me nothing" (ἐρωτήσετε) means asking questions; "ask the Father" (αἰτήσητε) means asking for something
alternatives: both mean making requests: in that day they will not make requests of Jesus but of the Father
decisions.reason: The first verb is the one used in verse 19, where the disciples wanted to question Jesus, and in 16:5 and 16:30 for questioning him. The second is the ordinary verb for asking for something, the one used for prayer in 14:13-14, 15:7, 16 and verse 24. So Jesus most likely means: in that day you will have no more questions for me, and whatever you ask for, the Father will give. But the first verb can also mean a request (14:16; 16:26), and some take both halves to be about prayer.

decisions.choice: in that day: the time after Jesus is raised, when they see him again and the Spirit teaches them
decisions.reason: "That day" (14:20) is the time that begins when he comes to them again (verse 22). Then the Spirit will guide them into all the truth (16:13; 14:26), and Jesus will speak to them plainly about the Father (16:25); their puzzled questions of verses 17-19 will be answered.

decisions.choice: he will give you in my name (SBLGNT): "in my name" goes with the giving
alternatives: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you (many manuscripts)
decisions.reason: In the SBLGNT, supported by some of the oldest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, "in my name" comes after "he will give you": the Father gives in Jesus's name. Many other manuscripts, among them Codex Alexandrinus and most later ones, put "in my name" before "he will give you", so that it is the asking that is done in his name, as in 14:13-14, 15:16 and verse 24. The difference is real but small, since both the asking and the giving rest on Jesus. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: he will give in my name: the Father gives for Jesus's sake and through him
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person (see 14:13). The Father's gifts come to the disciples on account of Jesus and through him; the next verse adds that they are to ask in his name too. Asking and giving both rest on him.

decisions.choice: you will not ask me any questions (B); you will have no more questions to ask me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that the first "ask" is about questions (meaning decision m1), so that it is not confused with asking the Father for things in the next sentence. Readable's "no more" connects the promise to the puzzled questions of verses 17-19. Literal keeps the same word "ask" for both verbs. "Truly, truly" is rendered as in verse 20.

records.greek: ἕως ἄρτι οὐκ ᾐτήσατε οὐδὲν ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου· αἰτεῖτε καὶ λήμψεσθε, ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ὑμῶν ᾖ πεπληρωμένη.
records.gloss: Until now not you asked nothing in the name of me; ask and you will receive, so that the joy of you may be having been made full.

L.24: Until now you have asked nothing in My name; ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be made full.

R.24: Up to now you have never asked for anything in My name. Keep asking, and you will receive, so that your joy will be full.

decisions.choice: until now: while Jesus was with them they asked him directly; asking in his name belongs to the time after he goes to the Father
decisions.reason: During his ministry the disciples brought their needs to Jesus himself. Asking the Father in Jesus's name is new: it belongs to the time when he has gone to the Father (14:12-14; 15:16; 16:26). "In my name" means asking as those who belong to him, on the ground of who he is (see 14:13).

decisions.choice: ask and you will receive: a standing invitation to keep asking
decisions.reason: The command "ask" (αἰτεῖτε) is in the present tense, which suits a continuing practice: go on asking. The promise "you will receive" answers it, as in Matthew 7:7-8.

decisions.choice: so that your joy may be complete: the same joy Jesus promised in 15:11
decisions.reason: "Made full" (πεπληρωμένη) is the verb of 15:11 and 17:13, here in a perfect form: a joy filled and staying full. Answered prayer is one way the joy of verse 22 is made complete.

decisions.choice: your joy may be made full (L); your joy will be complete (B); your joy will be full (R)
decisions.reason: The same wording as 15:11 at each level, since Jesus repeats that promise here. "Joy" is the key term at every level. Readable says "Keep asking" for the present-tense command (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: Ταῦτα ἐν παροιμίαις λελάληκα ὑμῖν· ἔρχεται ὥρα ὅτε οὐκέτι ἐν παροιμίαις λαλήσω ὑμῖν ἀλλὰ παρρησίᾳ περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀπαγγελῶ ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: "These things in figures of speech I have spoken to you; is coming an hour when no longer in figures of speech I will speak to you, but plainly concerning the Father I will report to you.

L.25: "These things I have spoken to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech, but I will report to you plainly about the Father.

R.25: "I have been telling you these things in pictures. But an hour is coming when I will stop speaking to you in pictures. Then I will tell you clearly about the Father.

decisions.choice: figures of speech: veiled sayings whose meaning has to be worked out
alternatives: parables in the sense of the stories in the other Gospels
decisions.reason: The same word described the picture of the shepherd and the sheep (10:6). Here it covers the images of the farewell talk: the Father's house with many rooms (14:2), the vine and the branches (15:1-8), the woman in labor (16:21), and the sayings about going away and coming back after "a little while" (16:16-19), which the disciples could not understand.

decisions.choice: plainly: in clear, direct words, without figures
decisions.reason: The word can mean speaking in public (7:26) or speaking with confidence, but here it is set against figures of speech, as in 10:24 and 11:14, so it means plain speech. The disciples pick up the same two words in 16:29.

decisions.choice: the coming hour: the time after Jesus's death and return to the Father, when the Spirit teaches them
alternatives: the rest of this same conversation
the hour of his death only
decisions.reason: Jesus has said that the Spirit will teach them everything and remind them of what he said (14:26) and guide them into all the truth (16:13); after the resurrection they understood what they had not understood before (2:22; 12:16). The "day" of 16:23 and 16:26 is the same time. In 16:29 the disciples think this hour has already arrived, and Jesus's answer (16:31-32) shows that it has not.

decisions.choice: report: announce, bring word
decisions.reason: The verb is used of bringing news or a message (4:51; 1 John 1:2-3). Jesus will make the Father known openly, as the one who has come from him (1:18).

decisions.choice: figures of speech (L, B), pictures (R); plainly (L), in plain words (B), clearly (R)
decisions.reason: The same English as 10:6 for the figure of speech and 10:24 for plainly, so that readers can follow John's thread from those chapters to 16:29. Readable uses the plain words it used there.

decisions.choice: hour, at every level
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John (12:23; 13:1), "hour" is kept at every level so that the thread of Jesus's appointed time stays visible. The Greek has no article, so the English says "an hour", as in 4:21 and 5:25.

records.heading: I have overcome the world

records.greek: ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου αἰτήσεσθε, καὶ οὐ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐρωτήσω τὸν πατέρα περὶ ὑμῶν·
records.gloss: In that the day in the name of me you will ask, and not I say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you;

L.26: In that day you will ask in My name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father concerning you;

R.26: When that day comes, you will make your requests in My name. And I am not saying that I myself will ask the Father for you.

decisions.choice: in that day: the time after the resurrection, the coming hour of 16:25
decisions.reason: The phrase points back to 16:23 and to 14:20, "In that day you will know that I am in my Father". It is the time after Jesus has gone to the Father and has come back to them, not the end of the age.

decisions.choice: ask in my name: ask the Father as people who belong to Jesus, on his authority
alternatives: use Jesus's name as a formula
decisions.reason: As in 14:13-14 and 16:23-24, asking in Jesus's name means coming to the Father as his disciples, in keeping with who he is. The verb here is the ordinary word for making a request.

decisions.choice: not a denial that Jesus prays for them, but a statement that the Father needs no persuading
alternatives: Jesus will no longer pray for his disciples
decisions.reason: Jesus does pray for them, in the very next chapter (17:9, 15, 20), and elsewhere the New Testament speaks of him interceding for his people (Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1). The point here is the reason Jesus gives at once: the Father himself loves them (16:27). They will not need a go-between to win over a reluctant Father.

decisions.choice: ask: make a request on someone's behalf
decisions.reason: This verb can mean to ask a question (16:19, 23, 30) or to make a request (14:16; 17:9). With "concerning you" it is a request: speaking to the Father for them.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Jesus or for the Father uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself and "you" when the disciples speak to him (16:29-30). At the start of a sentence the pronoun is written plain. This applies throughout 16:25-33.

decisions.choice: on your behalf (B), for you (R)
decisions.reason: "Concerning you" is word for word; with a verb of asking it means speaking for them, so Balanced and Readable say so.

records.greek: αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ φιλεῖ ὑμᾶς, ὅτι ὑμεῖς ἐμὲ πεφιλήκατε καὶ πεπιστεύκατε ὅτι ἐγὼ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξῆλθον.
records.gloss: Himself for the Father loves you, because you me have loved and have believed that I from the God came out.

L.27: for the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came out from God.

R.27: The Father Himself loves you. He loves you because you have come to love Me and to believe that I came from God.

decisions.choice: love: the same love as elsewhere in John, though the verb differs
alternatives: a warmer or lesser love of friendship, set against another verb for love
decisions.reason: John has two verbs for love and uses both of the Father's love for the Son (3:35; 5:20). Here he uses the one often linked with friendship, both for the Father's love and for the disciples' love of Jesus. The thought is the same as 14:21 and 14:23, where the other verb is used: the Father loves those who love the Son.

decisions.choice: the Father himself: of his own accord, without being persuaded
alternatives: the Father as well as Jesus
decisions.reason: The pronoun stands first for emphasis and answers 16:26: Jesus need not ask the Father for them, because the Father himself already loves them.

decisions.choice: because: their love and belief are the ground on which the Father's love meets them, not a payment that earns it
alternatives: the Father began to love them only when they loved Jesus
decisions.reason: The two verbs are perfect tenses: they have come to love Jesus and to believe, and they still do. John says elsewhere that God loved the world first (3:16; 1 John 4:10, 19). What is said here is that those who receive the Son are loved by the Father as the Son's own (14:21, 23; 17:23).

decisions.choice: from God, as in the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Some early and important manuscripts read "from the Father", which matches the next verse; others, also early, read "from God", which the SBLGNT follows. Copyists could easily have brought this verse into line with 16:28. The sense is the same either way. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: came out from (L, B), came from (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to go out or come out; Literal and Balanced say "came out from" as in 8:42, so that readers see the picture of coming out from the Father's presence. Readable says it simply.

decisions.choice: The Father himself loves you. He loves you because ...
alternatives: For the Father himself loves you, because ...
decisions.reason: Readable begins a new sentence and repeats "he loves you" so that the reason can stand on its own. The link with 16:26 is still clear from the order of the sentences. "Have come to love ... and to believe" brings out the perfect tenses (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἐξῆλθον ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ ἐλήλυθα εἰς τὸν κόσμον· πάλιν ἀφίημι τὸν κόσμον καὶ πορεύομαι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα.
records.gloss: I came out from the Father and have come into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father."

L.28: I came out from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and going to the Father."

R.28: I came from the Father and came into the world. Now I am leaving the world and going back to the Father."

decisions.choice: the first clause, "I came out from the Father", is part of the text, as in the SBLGNT
alternatives: the verse begins "and I have come into the world"
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and a few other witnesses, including some Old Latin manuscripts, lack the first clause. Most manuscripts have it. Copyists may have left it out because it seemed to repeat the end of 16:27. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: again: in turn, going back the way he came
decisions.reason: Jesus is not leaving the world for a second time. "Again" marks the reverse movement: he came from the Father into the world, and now he leaves the world for the Father. The verse sums up the whole Gospel (1:1, 14; 13:1, 3).

decisions.choice: I leave, I go: the present tense for a departure already under way
decisions.reason: The departure is still ahead, but Jesus speaks of it as already happening, as in 14:28 and 16:5. The hour has come (13:1).

decisions.choice: the world: the human world into which the Son came
alternatives: the world as hostile to God
decisions.reason: Here the world is the place and people to whom the Son was sent (1:9-10; 3:17), not, as in 16:33, humanity set against God. World is a key term.

decisions.choice: Now, in turn (B); going back (R)
decisions.reason: "Again" could be read as a second departure; Balanced and Readable give the sense of reversing the journey (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable add "now" for the change from his coming to his going.

decisions.choice: I am leaving ... going
decisions.reason: The English progressive shows a departure that is about to happen and has in a sense begun (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: Λέγουσιν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ· Ἴδε νῦν ἐν παρρησίᾳ λαλεῖς, καὶ παροιμίαν οὐδεμίαν λέγεις.
records.gloss: Say the disciples of him, "Look, now in plainness you speak, and figure of speech none you say.

L.29: His disciples say, "Look, now You are speaking plainly, and You are saying no figure of speech.

R.29: Then His disciples said, "Now You are speaking clearly! You are not using pictures anymore.

decisions.choice: the disciples think the promised hour of plain speech has already come
alternatives: they rightly see that Jesus has now spoken plainly
decisions.reason: Jesus said that an hour is coming when he will speak plainly (16:25); the disciples answer "now". Jesus has indeed said something direct (16:28), but his reply (16:31-32) shows that they have not yet understood what is about to happen. Their "now" is said too soon.

decisions.choice: plainly and figure of speech: the same two words as 16:25
decisions.reason: The disciples repeat Jesus's words, setting plain speech against figures, as in 10:6 and 10:24.

decisions.choice: look: a call to attention
alternatives: see, an order to look at something
decisions.reason: The word draws attention to what they think has just happened. It does not ask anyone to see something with the eyes.

decisions.choice: Historic present: say (L); said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John tells this past event in the present tense ("his disciples say") to make it vivid. Literal keeps the present so that readers see the Greek form; Balanced and Readable use the past, the normal tense for telling a story in English. This decision applies to the historic present in 16:25-33.

decisions.choice: plainly (L), in plain words (B), clearly (R); figure of speech (L, B), pictures (R)
decisions.reason: The same English as in 16:25, so that readers hear the disciples repeat Jesus's words.

records.greek: νῦν οἴδαμεν ὅτι οἶδας πάντα καὶ οὐ χρείαν ἔχεις ἵνα τίς σε ἐρωτᾷ· ἐν τούτῳ πιστεύομεν ὅτι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἐξῆλθες.
records.gloss: Now we know that you know all things and not need you have that anyone you should question; by this we believe that from God you came out."

L.30: Now we know that You know all things and have no need that anyone question You; by this we believe that You came out from God."

R.30: Now we know that You know everything. You do not need anyone to ask You questions. That is why we believe that You came from God."

decisions.choice: no need that anyone question you: Jesus knows their questions before they ask them
alternatives: no need for anyone to teach you
decisions.reason: Jesus answered the question they wanted to ask (16:17-19) before they put it to him. He knows what is in people (2:24-25; 1:48). The disciples take this as proof that he knows all things.

decisions.choice: question: ask questions of someone
decisions.reason: The same verb meant making a request in 16:26; here, as in 16:19 and 16:23, it means asking questions.

decisions.choice: by this: because of this, on this ground
alternatives: in this, in the sense of in this matter
decisions.reason: "This" is Jesus's knowledge of their thoughts. It is the reason they give for believing.

decisions.choice: a true confession, but not yet a full understanding
decisions.reason: They say what Jesus said in 16:27, and it is true (17:8). But they believe on the strength of what they have just seen, and Jesus's next words test it (16:31-32).

decisions.choice: This is why (B); That is why (R)
decisions.reason: "In this" or "by this" is word for word; Balanced and Readable give the causal sense plainly (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς Ἰησοῦς· Ἄρτι πιστεύετε;
records.gloss: Answered them Jesus, "Now do you believe?

L.31: Jesus answered them, "Now do you believe?

R.31: Jesus answered them, "Do you believe now?

decisions.choice: a question, as the SBLGNT punctuates it
decisions.reason: The Greek has no punctuation of its own, and the words could be a question or a statement. Taken as a question, Jesus asks whether their belief is as firm as they think. Taken as a statement, he grants that they believe, and the next verse shows how soon it will be tested. Either way the following words are a warning, not a rejection: he goes on to promise them peace (16:33).

decisions.choice: now: at this moment, picking up the disciples' own "now"
decisions.reason: The disciples twice said "now" (16:29, 30). Jesus's word, placed first, takes it up: at this very point, when the hour of their scattering is about to come (16:32).

decisions.choice: a testing of their belief, not a denial that they believe
alternatives: Jesus dismisses their belief as false
decisions.reason: Jesus answered Peter's promise in the same way (13:37-38). He has just said that they have believed (16:27); what he questions is whether they understand what is coming.

decisions.choice: Do you believe now?
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "now" first, as in the Greek. Balanced and Readable use ordinary English order; a reader aloud can still stress "now".

records.greek: ἰδοὺ ἔρχεται ὥρα καὶ ἐλήλυθεν ἵνα σκορπισθῆτε ἕκαστος εἰς τὰ ἴδια κἀμὲ μόνον ἀφῆτε· καὶ οὐκ εἰμὶ μόνος, ὅτι ὁ πατὴρ μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Look, is coming an hour and has come that you be scattered each to the own [things] and me alone you leave; and not I am alone, because the Father with me is.

L.32: Look, an hour is coming and has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own [home], and will leave Me alone; and I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.

R.32: Look, an hour is coming, and it is already here, when you will all run off, each to his own home. You will leave Me all alone. But I am not alone. The Father is with Me.

decisions.choice: the hour: Jesus's hour, the time of his arrest and death, now arriving
decisions.reason: "Is coming and has come" is said as in 4:23 and 5:25. This is the hour of 12:23, 12:27 and 13:1, so near that it has in effect begun; that same night the disciples will scatter at his arrest.

decisions.choice: an echo of Zechariah 13:7, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered
alternatives: no allusion; scattered is simply the natural word
decisions.reason: In Mark 14:27 and Matthew 26:31 Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7, "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered", on the same night. John does not quote it, but he uses the same verb for scattering, and he has used it of the wolf scattering the sheep (10:12). The echo is likely but not certain.

decisions.choice: each to his own: each one going off to his own home or his own place
alternatives: each back to his own former life
decisions.reason: The phrase, "to the own things", means one's own home or place, as in 19:27, where the disciple takes Jesus's mother "to his own". It pictures the group breaking up as each one goes his own way.

decisions.choice: Jesus is not alone, because the Father is with him even when the disciples leave
decisions.reason: Jesus said the same in 8:16 and 8:29, "The one who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone." The "and" here has the force of "yet": the disciples will leave him, but the Father will not.

decisions.choice: each to his own [home] (L); each to his own home (B, R)
alternatives: each to their own home (under the gender setting)
decisions.reason: Jesus is speaking to the eleven disciples, specific men, so "his" is plain and takes no gender setting (style guide, section 6). Literal brackets "home", which the Greek leaves understood ("to his own things").

decisions.choice: [home] (L); home (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "his own" with a plural article ("the own things"); English needs a noun, and "home" gives the sense of meaning decision m3. Readable says "run off" for the scattering, which is what they did at the arrest.

records.greek: ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν ἵνα ἐν ἐμοὶ εἰρήνην ἔχητε· ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ θλῖψιν ἔχετε, ἀλλὰ θαρσεῖτε, ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον.
records.gloss: These things I have spoken to you so that in me peace you may have; in the world affliction you have, but have courage, I have overcome the world."

L.33: These things I have spoken to you so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you have affliction; but have courage, I have overcome the world."

R.33: I have told you all this so that you can have peace in Me. In the world you have trouble. But be brave! I have already won the victory over the world."

decisions.choice: you have, present tense, as in the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "you will have"; the present is well attested in the earliest manuscripts. The present says that affliction is already part of life in the world for Jesus's followers, as 15:18-16:4 has described. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: affliction: pressure and distress, especially the hostility the disciples will meet
alternatives: the great tribulation at the end of the age
decisions.reason: The word means being pressed hard. In 16:21 it is the pain of a woman giving birth; in the farewell talk it is the hatred and persecution the world will bring (15:18-20; 16:2). It is not here a technical term for the end times.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity set against God, the source of the disciples' affliction
decisions.reason: "In me" and "in the world" are set side by side: peace in Jesus, affliction in the world. The world here is the world that hates Jesus and his disciples (15:18-19), whose ruler has been judged (16:11). World is a key term.

decisions.choice: I have overcome: a victory already won, spoken before the cross
decisions.reason: The verb is in the perfect tense, used of a completed act whose result stands. Jesus speaks on the eve of his death as one who has already won. The same verb is used of the believer's victory over the world, which comes through him (1 John 5:4-5). The "I" is emphatic.

decisions.choice: have courage (L, B); be brave (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to be bold or confident in the face of danger. "Be of good cheer" now sounds like a call to be cheerful, which is not the point. "Have courage" says the sense in ordinary words; Readable says it more simply still.

decisions.choice: affliction (L, B), trouble (R); overcome (L, B), already won the victory over (R)
decisions.reason: "Tribulation" now suggests the end times to many readers (meaning decision m2); "affliction" keeps the sense of pressure from outside. "Overcome" is the word of 1 John 5:4-5 for the same verb. Readable adds "already" to bring out the perfect tense (meaning decision m4).
